lines: Only thirty-five percent of companies that started onboarding to the Microsoft Store ever finished.
For individual developers, it was ninety.
Companies paid a ninety-nine dollar fee before they knew if they could pass, and one in three stopped right there.
Requirements surfaced late, progress was invisible, and about forty-one percent failed vetting, often with no reason given.
First, we moved onboarding into a Store-owned flow.
That let us drop the ninety-nine dollar fee, sign companies in with Microsoft Entra, and explain what verification needs before anyone commits.
Then I replaced one rigid path with three ways to verify.
Upload a business document, and AI pre-fills the company details for review, with people still in the loop.
And failure became a step, not an ending.
Email and domain are checked before anything is submitted, status updates live with a clear reason, and companies fix issues without starting over.
After a pilot in fifty countries, it rolled out to every Store market.
Onboarding success went from thirty-five to seventy-three percent, and vetting time fell from about fifteen days to one.
The best onboarding doesn't remove complexity from the system.
It absorbs it, so the user doesn't have to.
